cls: Topical antiseptic / oxidizing oral debriding agent
pharm: Releases oxygen on contact with tissue catalase, producing effervescence that mechanically loosens debris and exerts weak, transient antimicrobial action.
quick: First aid (3%): apply a small amount to the area 1-3 times daily. Oral rinse: dilute 1:1 with water, swish >=1 min, spit, up to 4 times/day
Oral rinse used after meals and at bedtime; not swallowed
Topical/oral-rinse use at 3% is considered low risk; minimal systemic absorption
Topical/oral-rinse use is considered compatible; negligible systemic exposure
No interaction at OTC topical/oral concentrations
Watch wound healing and for persistent irritation; none systemic for OTC use
summary: Hydrogen peroxide (stabilized 3%) is an over-the-counter first-aid antiseptic and oral debriding agent. On contact with tissue catalase it rapidly releases oxygen, and the resulting effervescence mechanically loosens debris while providing weak, short-lived antimicrobial activity. It is for external use only - used on minor cuts, scrapes and burns, or diluted as a mouth rinse for minor mouth irritation. It should not be used in the eyes, on large body areas for more than a week, or for deep/puncture wounds, animal bites or serious burns without medical advice. Concentrated solutions are corrosive and can cause serious injury or gas embolism if ingested.
indications: First aid to help prevent the risk of infection in minor cuts, scrapes and burns
Oral debriding agent / aids removal of phlegm, mucus or other secretions associated with occasional sore mouth

dosage.n: External use only; do not use over large areas longer than 1 week

dosage.t: Up to 4 times daily after meals and at bedtime
dosage.n: Do not swallow; use up to 7 days

admin: For external use only; do not use in the eyes
Clean the affected area before applying a small amount to minor wounds
For oral use, dilute 1:1 with water, swish, and spit out - do not swallow

Hold the bottle away from the face when opening and keep it tightly closed in a cool, dark place; do not shake
moa: Hydrogen peroxide is an oxidizing antiseptic. When it contacts tissue and blood, the enzyme catalase rapidly decomposes it into water and molecular oxygen. The released oxygen produces effervescence that mechanically dislodges debris, pus and necrotic tissue from wounds, and the oxidizing action and brief release of reactive oxygen species provide a weak, transient antimicrobial effect against bacteria, viruses and fungi. Its antiseptic potency is limited and short-lived because catalase inactivates it quickly.

absolute: Application to deep/puncture wounds, serious burns or animal bites without medical advice
relative: Use in closed body cavities or under pressure (gas embolism risk)
monitor: Wound healing and signs of irritation
Persistence or worsening of mouth or skin symptoms
Development of swelling, rash, or fever

preg: Topical and diluted oral-rinse use of 3% hydrogen peroxide is considered low risk in pregnancy because systemic absorption is negligible. Avoid swallowing and use as directed.
lact: Topical and oral-rinse use is regarded as compatible with breastfeeding, as it is rapidly broken down and minimally absorbed; avoid application to the nipple area before feeds.
renal: Not relevant for topical or oral-rinse use; there is no meaningful systemic exposure.
hepatic: Not relevant for topical or oral-rinse use; there is no meaningful systemic exposure.

minor: Activity is reduced in the presence of organic matter and is inactivated by tissue catalase; do not combine with other wound chemicals
interactions.food: Oral rinse is used after meals and at bedtime; do not swallow.
interactions.diagnostics: Can cause artifactual oxygen bubbles or interfere with some microbiological wound cultures if applied before sampling.

common: Transient bleaching/whitening of skin or mucosa
Mild burning of the mouth (oral rinse)
serious: Delayed wound healing/tissue irritation with repeated use
rare: Gas embolism if instilled into closed cavities or deep wounds under pressure
Black hairy tongue with prolonged oral use
emergency: Ingestion of concentrated (high-strength) solution causing corrosive injury or gas embolism
Air embolism after irrigation of deep/closed wounds

monitoring: Healing of treated wound or mouth area
Signs of persistent irritation, pain or redness
New swelling, rash or fever (stop and seek care)
counsel: Use only on the skin or as a diluted mouth rinse - do not swallow it and keep it out of the eyes
It may fizz, sting briefly, and temporarily whiten the skin - this is expected
Do not use on deep wounds, animal bites or serious burns, or over large areas for more than a week, without seeing a doctor
Stop and see a doctor if redness, pain, swelling, rash or fever develops, or mouth symptoms last more than 7 days
Keep the bottle tightly closed in a cool, dark place, out of reach of children
pk: Acts immediately on contact (effervescence within seconds)
Rapid; oxygen release peaks on contact with tissue catalase
Very short - decomposed almost instantly by tissue catalase
Keep tightly closed in a cool, dark place; do not shake the bottle; hold away from the face when opening
pearls: Antimicrobial effect is weak and brief because tissue catalase inactivates it almost instantly
Mechanical debridement from effervescence is its main practical benefit on wounds
Repeated use can be cytotoxic to fibroblasts and delay healing - not for routine cleaning of clean granulating wounds
Never instill under pressure into deep or closed wounds/cavities - oxygen gas embolism has occurred
Concentrated (e.g., 35% 'food-grade') solutions are corrosive and dangerous if ingested
missed: Not applicable; hydrogen peroxide is used as needed for first aid or as a mouth rinse rather than on a fixed dosing schedule.
overdose: Topical overuse causes local irritation and delayed healing. Ingestion of household 3% solution usually causes only mild GI upset and foaming, but ingestion of concentrated solutions can cause corrosive injury, severe gastric distension, and life-threatening oxygen gas embolism. For ingestion, do not induce vomiting; give supportive care, dilute with water/milk for low-concentration ingestion, and seek urgent medical/poison-center evaluation (imaging and hyperbaric oxygen may be needed for embolism).
